name: Kansas City, Mexico & Orient Railway of Texas
description: The former Orient route grew into a substantial 603-mile railroad across West Texas after Santa Fe acquired control in 1928. Panhandle & Santa Fe operated the property with Santa Fe personnel and equipment, while Kansas City, Mexico & Orient Railway Company of Texas remained the corporate owner and lessor until its August 1, 1965 merger into ATSF. It had no separate diesel fleet.

statistics.intro: Two snapshots describe the resources serving the 603-mile former Orient operating territory, not equipment legally owned by KCM&O of Texas or audited corporate employee counts. Values marked ~ are project estimates supplied for this comparison.

snapshots.label: Early Documented Diesel Operation

locomotives.note: Mixed steam/diesel operating requirement during transition; Santa Fe-supplied power.

snapshots.context: The January 25, 1951 Eldorado Success documents diesel operation from San Angelo toward Eldorado. Local histories place the Orient–Santa Fe steam-to-diesel transition in the 1950s; this is an early diesel snapshot, not a claim of complete dieselization or the first diesel ever used.

snapshots.label: Final Full Year

locomotives.note: Diesel operating requirement / equivalent fleet supplied by Santa Fe.

snapshots.context: 1964 was the final complete year before the August 1, 1965 merger. Dieselization, declining passenger service and reduced servicing infrastructure lowered staffing needs. San Angelo’s former 17-stall roundhouse was demolished in 1962. Santa Fe GP7 No. 2867 was photographed at Presidio in 1961, directly documenting diesel road power on former Orient territory.

notes: Employees: a 1928 contemporary report described a threatened strike involving 600 KCM&O employees across the U.S. system; this was not a total-workforce census. Texas held a large majority of U.S. mileage, and local history reports more than 200 Santa Fe workers at San Angelo during WWII. ~900 includes train crews, maintenance-of-way, station, shop, signal and clerical staff across 603 miles; ~550 reflects dieselization, declining passenger service and reduced servicing infrastructure. These are order-of-magnitude operating estimates, not audited KCM&O corporate counts.

Locomotives: ~35 in 1951 and ~30 in 1964 estimate Santa Fe power serving the territory, not a KCM&O-owned fleet. The supplied system-density allocation, reduced substantially for secondary, light-density operations, remains unverified. San Angelo’s former 17-stall roundhouse is a scale check, not a fleet census.

Non-locomotive rolling stock: ~1,700 in each year is an operating-fleet equivalent from Santa Fe freight, passenger and company-service car totals, adjusted downward for lighter traffic. This allocation remains unverified; it represents neither KCM&O ownership nor cars simultaneously on the line.

Capitalization: ~$9M is a comparative property-value proxy derived from the verified acquisition-era ICC valuation, not contemporaneous 1951/1964 accounting capitalization. The Supreme Court publication cites a Texas property valuation of $6,854,522 including expenditures for additions before the 1930 extensions. Simple mileage scaling from ~465 to ~603 miles gives ~$6.85M × 603 / 465 ≈ $8.9M, rounded to ~$9M for both snapshots. This common comparison baseline does not establish unchanged property value between 1951 and 1964 or verified capital stock plus funded debt.

history: The Texas component of the Orient system was renamed Kansas City, Mexico & Orient Railway Company of Texas in 1905. Its route linked the Red River, Sweetwater, San Angelo and Alpine. Santa Fe acquired the Orient on October 19, 1928; after completing the Presidio and Sonora extensions in 1930, it leased the Texas property to Panhandle & Santa Fe for operation effective January 1, 1931.

In 1930, approximately 72 miles from Paisano to Presidio and 65 miles from San Angelo to Sonora were added. The mature Texas system comprised approximately 603 route miles. KCM&O of Texas survived as a separate legal owner and lessor through the diesel era, merging into the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railway on August 1, 1965.
paintSchemesIntro: KCM&O of Texas did not maintain a separate diesel-era paint identity after Santa Fe acquired the Orient. Panhandle & Santa Fe operated the property with Santa Fe locomotives and equipment, which carried standard Santa Fe paint schemes. See the Santa Fe page for the shared system paint history.
